questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The structure marked in the given picture arises from the _______.
questions.explanation: The marked structure is the fornix. It arises from the hippocampus and ends in the mammillary body of the hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: An infant is referred to neurology due to an abnormal MRI report as shown below. What is the most anterior part of the missing brain structure?
questions.explanation: The MRI is suggestive of total agenesis of the corpus callosum. The most anterior part of the corpus callosum is the genu. The source contrasts a normal sagittal MRI with complete agenesis of the corpus callosum.

questions.question: What is the area marked as 'A' in the image below?
questions.explanation: The area marked A is the rostrum of the corpus callosum. It connects the orbital surfaces of the frontal lobes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: An infant is brought to the casualty with the symptom given below. MRI revealed the agenesis of a crucial cranial structure. Which part of this structure give rise to tapetum?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario with infantile spasms is suggestive of Aicardi syndrome, an X-linked dominant disorder associated with agenesis of the corpus callosum. The fibres of the tapetum originate from both the body and splenium of the corpus callosum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is connected to the structure marked as A in the image below?
questions.explanation: The structure marked A is the splenium of the corpus callosum and it is connected to the striate cortex. Fibers from the splenium form the forceps major and arch backward into the occipital lobe. The hippocampus lies inferior to the splenium but is not directly connected to it.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A woman presented with split-brain syndrome following an experimental brain surgery to manage severe epileptic seizures. Which fibres constitute the surgically resected structure?
questions.explanation: Split-brain syndrome can follow corpus callosotomy. Commissural fibres constitute the corpus callosum. Corpus callosotomy is used as a last-resort procedure for intractable epileptic seizures and can produce disconnection between the two cerebral hemispheres.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The cingulum of the brain is classified under ____________.
questions.explanation: The cingulum is a long association fiber. It lies within the cingulate gyrus and connects frontal and parietal lobes with parahippocampal and temporal cortical regions.
questions.structuredExplanationText: The cingulum is a long association fiber. It lies within the cingulate gyrus and connects frontal and parietal lobes with parahippocampal and temporal cortical regions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Following road traffic accident, a man developed head injury resulting in a defect in the association fibres. Which of the following is not classified under these fibres?
questions.explanation: Corona radiata is not an association fiber; it is a projection fiber. Cingulum is a long association fiber connecting frontal and parietal lobes with parahippocampal and temporal regions. The source classifies the fornix as an association fiber while noting that the hippocampal commissure of the fornix contains commissural fibers. Arcuate fasciculus is listed as a short association fiber in this source.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A woman presented with self-inflicted injuries, auditory hallucinations and delusions. MRI revealed a tumour involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the structure medial to it. Which structure is likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: The thalamus lies medial to the posterior limb of the internal capsule. The internal capsule separates the thalamus and caudate nucleus from the lentiform nucleus. In horizontal section it is V-shaped and includes anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolenticular part and sublenticular part. The anterior limb lies between the caudate head medially and lentiform nucleus laterally; the posterior limb lies between the thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally.

The anterior limb lies between the caudate head medially and lentiform nucleus laterally; the posterior limb lies between the thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A man presented with dysarthria suggestive of a lesion involving the corticonuclear tract. MRI revealed an ischemic stroke. Which part(s) of the internal capsule were most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Corticonuclear fibres pass through the genu of the internal capsule. Most corticonuclear fibers cross in the median plane before supplying cranial nerve nuclei. Cranial motor nuclei receive bilateral corticonuclear connections except the facial nucleus supplying the lower face and the hypoglossal nucleus supplying genioglossus. The anterior limb carries frontopontine fibers; the posterior limb carries corticospinal motor fibers anteriorly and sensory fibers posteriorly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: An 81-year-old man presented with ipsilateral paralysis. Examination showed hypertonia, hyperreflexia and the following finding. Which region of white matter does not contain the damaged fibres?

options.text: Lateral white column of the spinal cord
Anterior limb of the internal capsule

questions.correctAnswerText: Anterior limb of the internal capsule
questions.explanation: The scenario with paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia and ankle clonus is suggestive of corticospinal tract involvement. The anterior limb of the internal capsule does not contain corticospinal fibres; these pass through the posterior limb. The corticospinal tract also traverses the cerebral peduncle, pyramids of the medulla and lateral white column of the spinal cord.
questions.structuredExplanationText: The scenario with paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia and ankle clonus is suggestive of corticospinal tract involvement. questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the structures which consist of commissural fibres:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A, B and C only. In the source diagram: A is the corpus callosum, B is the anterior commissure, C is the posterior commissure and D is the body of the fornix. The body of the fornix mainly contains association fibres, while the commissure of the fornix (hippocampal commissure) contains commissural fibers. The source notes differing textbook classification of the fornix.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The habenular commissure is located in the _________.
questions.explanation: The habenular commissure is located in the superior lamina of the pineal gland. The source lists locations of commissural fibers: corpus callosum on the medial surface of the brain; anterior commissure beneath the rostrum of corpus callosum; posterior commissure in the inferior lamina of the pineal gland; habenular commissure in the superior lamina; and hippocampal commissure between the right and left fornices.

questions.explanation: The arrow indicates the fornix. It arises from the hippocampus and ends in the mammillary body of the hypothalamus. The source classifies the fornix here as an association fiber and states that it is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the areas marked in the given image?

options.text: A is a type of association fiber
C is content of interpeduncular fossa
D is devoid of blood brain barrier

questions.correctAnswerText: A is a type of association fiber
questions.explanation: A is the anterior commissure, which is a commissural fiber rather than an association fiber. B is the lamina terminalis. C is the mammillary body and is a content of the interpeduncular fossa. D is the pineal gland, which lacks a blood-brain barrier.
questions.structuredExplanationText: A is the anterior commissure, which is a commissural fiber rather than an association fiber. B is the lamina terminalis. C is the mammillary body and is a content of the interpeduncular fossa. D is the pineal gland, which lacks a blood-brain barrier.
